title: Between the Follower and the Followed
summary: Page-three editorial framed around Quran 2:166, in which followed leaders disown their followers on the Day of Judgement. Addressed primarily to foreign fighters (muhajireen) in Syria who pledged allegiance to Ahmad al-Sharaa (al-Julani) and the post-Assad leadership. Argues that the collapse of the previous regime was a 'temptation' that exposed those who abandoned the Islamic State project for a nationalist, party-political enterprise bounded by Syrian borders. Revives the anti-nationalist framework of the late IS spokesman al-Adnani to charge that any 'civil state' jihad is by definition outside the path. Accuses al-Sharaa of accommodation with Israel, the United States, and the broader 'Crusader' order, and of substituting civil law for sharia. Mocks muhajireen as 'twice-migrated', predicts they will be slaughtered or handed over by their new patrons, and exhorts them to abandon 'al-Julani's enclosure' and return to the Islamic State. Closes with the Quranic citation of leaders disowning their followers as bonds between them are severed.
keyClaims: Fighters who pledged allegiance to al-Sharaa were drawn into a civil-state, nationalist project rather than the path of the Islamic State.
The post-Assad Syrian leadership serves Crusader, Jewish, and American interests and is friendly to Israel.
al-Adnani's earlier warnings against party-political and border-bound jihad have been vindicated by events.
Foreign fighters under al-Sharaa's authority will ultimately be killed or handed over to their enemies.
Muhajireen should abandon the new Syrian project and return to the Islamic State.
significanceAssessment: Extends IS's sustained de-legitimisation campaign against al-Sharaa into a more targeted defection appeal aimed at the foreign-fighter cohort inside Syria. The deliberate revival of al-Adnani's anti-nationalist vocabulary indicates IS is consolidating a stable ideological frame around HTS's transition to statecraft, treating it as a 'told you so' moment to recruit from disillusioned muhajireen. The Quranic framing of betrayal at the Day of Judgement signals an eschatological register intended to deepen the sense of stakes for the target audience.
notes: Gregorian date converted from Hijri 26 Dhu al-Qa'da 1447. Page 3 editorial only; rest of issue not in screenshot.
